translations.text: Of our holy father John, formerly archbishop of Constantinople.
John Chrysostom. A sermon on the resurrection of our Lord on the third day. On Monday.
Today is a fitting time for all of us to proclaim what the blessed David said:
“Who will declare the mighty deeds of the Lord, or make all his praises heard?”
Behold, our beloved and saving feast has come to us: the day of the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ.
The cause of peace, the beginning of reconciliation, the removal of conflict, the destruction of death, the defeat of the devil.
Today angels have mingled with human beings, and those who bear bodies, together with the bodiless powers,
sing a song of praise. Today the devil’s opposition has been destroyed.
Today the bonds of death have been loosed; the victory of Hades has vanished.
Today is a fitting time to repeat that prophetic cry:
“Death, where is your sting? Hades, where is your victory?” Today our Master Christ shattered the bronze gates
and disfigured the very face of death. But why do I say its face? He changed its very name.
For death is no longer called death, but repose and sleep.
For before Christ’s coming and the Savior’s descent, even the name of death
was terrifying. For the first man who came into being was condemned by it as a great threat, when he heard:
“On the day you eat, you will surely die.” And the blessed Job called it by this name, saying:
“Death is rest for a man.” And the prophet David said, “The death of sinners is evil.”
The separation of the soul from the body was called not only death, but also Hades.
For listen to the patriarch Jacob saying, “You will bring my old age down to Hades in sorrow.”
And again, the prophet: “Hades opened its mouth wide.” And again, another prophet saying:
“He will deliver me from the lowest Hades.” And often in the ancient books you will find
the departure from here called death and Hades. But once the descent was completed,
the resurrection dawned, and the Master who loves humanity brought a new and wondrous way of living into our life.
For now, instead of death, the departure from here is called repose and sleep.
How, then, is this clear? Listen to him himself.
Christ saying, “Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I am going to awaken him.”
For just as it is easy for us to awaken someone and raise him up, so it is for our common Master
to raise the dead with his voice. And since what he said to them was new and astonishing,
even the disciples did not understand what was said until he stooped to their weakness and spoke plainly.
And the teacher of the whole world, blessed Paul, writing to the Thessalonians, said,
“I do not want you to be ignorant about those who have fallen asleep, so that you will not grieve like the others who have no hope.”
And again elsewhere: “Have those who have fallen asleep in Christ then perished?” And again: “We who are alive and remain
will not overtake those who have fallen asleep.” And elsewhere again: “For if we believe that Jesus
died and rose again, so too God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus.”
Do you see how death is now everywhere called slumber and sleep,
and how, though it formerly had a terrifying face, it became something we disregard after the resurrection?
Do you see how glorious the victory of the resurrection is? Through it, very many good things were brought in.
Through it, demonic deception was destroyed. Through it, we mock death.
Through it, we scorn this present life. Through it, we press on toward the things to come.
Through it, although we bear bodies, we lack nothing in comparison with bodiless beings, if we so desire.
Today our victories were small. Today our Master, having won victory over death
and destroyed the devil’s opposition, granted us the path to salvation through the resurrection. We all
therefore rejoice, leap for joy, and celebrate. For although our Master has conquered
and established the victory, the celebration and joy became common to us his servants as well. For it was for our salvation
that he did everything. And by the very means through which the devil defeated us, Christ overcame him.
He took up that very weapon and defeated him with it. How? Listen.
A virgin, a tree, and death were the signs of our defeat. For Eve was a virgin:
she had not known a man when she accepted the deception. There was a tree; the penalty imposed on Adam was death.
Do you see how a virgin, a tree, and death became signs of our defeat? Now see in turn
how these very same things also became signs of victory: Mary in place of Eve; in place of the tree,
to know and discern good and evil. The tree of the cross. In place of Adam’s death,
the Lord’s death. Do you see how he is defeated by the very means by which he conquered? Through a tree the devil overcame Adam.
Through the cross Christ overcame the devil. That tree sent people down into Hades,
but the tree of the cross called back from Hades even those who had departed. That tree hid him naked, like a captive,
but this tree displayed the victor to everyone, nailed naked on high. And death—that death
condemned even those who came after it. But this death, even those who departed before it,
has truly raised up. Who can tell of the Lord’s mighty deeds or make all his praises heard?
Through death we have become immortal. This is the achievement of the cross.
This is the great manifestation of the resurrection. Today the angels
rejoice, and all the heavenly powers are glad, delighting in the salvation of the whole human race.
For if there is joy in heaven and on earth over one sinner who repents,
how much more over the salvation of the whole world! Today, human nature,
he freed from the devil’s hostility and restored to its original nobility. For when I see my firstfruits
having thus overcome death, I am no longer afraid. I no longer fear the adversary,
nor do I look at my own weakness, but I consider the inexpressible power of the one who fights for me.
For he who overcame the hostility of death and took away all its strength—
what will he not do for his own kind, whose form he deigned in his great mercy to take on,
and in that form to wage war against the devil? Today there is joy everywhere throughout the world, and spiritual gladness.
The assembly of angels and all the powers above rejoice over humanity’s salvation. Consider, beloved, the greatness of this joy:
that [?] all the powers above celebrate with us. For they join in rejoicing over the good things that are ours.
For although the grace that comes from the Master is ours, it brings delight to them as well.
For this reason they are not ashamed to celebrate with us. The Master himself, theirs as well as ours, is not ashamed to celebrate with us.
But why did I say, “He is not ashamed”? He even desires to celebrate with us.
How is this evident? Listen to him himself saying, “I have earnestly desired
to eat this Passover with you.” If, then, he desired to eat the Passover,
It is clear that we too should join in the celebration. So when you see not only angels,
but also archangels and the whole assembly of the heavenly powers, and even the Lord of the angels himself celebrating with us,
what reason for joy do you lack? So let no one be downcast today
because of poverty, for this is a spiritual celebration. Let no one honor a rich man because of his wealth,
for he can bring none of his possessions into this celebration. At outward celebrations—
I mean worldly ones—where there is much display in outward clothing
and in the great variety of food on the table, the poor man is always despondent and sorrowful,
while the rich man enjoys pleasure and gladness. Why? Because the latter wears splendid clothing
and sets out a lavish table, while the poor man is prevented by poverty from showing the same affection.
But here there is nothing of the sort. Has not the same idleness [?] been cast out by everyone?
There is one table for both rich and poor, for slave and free. Even if you are rich,
you will have no advantage over the poor man. If you are poor, you will have no less than the rich man.
Nor will your spiritual joy be diminished because of poverty, for it is God's gift and recognizes no distinction between persons.
But why do I say that the same table is set before rich and poor? Even for the man who wears the crown and is clothed in purple,
who holds authority over the inhabited world,
and for the destitute man who begs for alms, the same table is set.
For such are spiritual gifts: participation is not allotted according to rank,
but according to willingness and choice. With the same confidence and honor,
both emperor and poor man approach to enjoy and partake of these divine mysteries.
But why do I say with the same honor? Often the poor approach with greater confidence.
Why? Because the emperor, held captive by concerns about his possessions and surrounded by many troubles,
is like someone out on the open sea: he is beset [?] by all kinds of different waves and adds many sins.
But the poor man is free from all this.
He is concerned only with the food he needs, and lives a life free from worry and sorrow,
as though sitting in a harbor, in calm waters, with great reverence.
approaches the table. And not only this, but also from many other things
various kinds of despondency arise in those celebrating the festival.
On worldly festivals. But [?] there, the poor man is in distress,
while the rich man rejoices, not only because of the table and its abundance, but also because of splendid clothes
and the magnificence of his clothing. What they suffer because of the table, they also experience because of clothes.
For when the poor man sees the rich man dressed in expensive clothing,
he is pierced with sorrow, laments his own lot, and imagines countless things. But here
even despondency itself has been taken away. For everyone has one and the same robe, the clothing of salvation.
And Paul cries out, saying, “All of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ.”
Let us not disgrace this festival, I beg you, but let us embrace a wisdom worthy of what has been given to us through the spiritual gift.
Let us not surrender ourselves to drunkenness and gluttony, but let us recognize the honor our Master has shown us,
for he honored the rich equally, and slaves and free people, and poured out a common gift upon everyone.
Let us offer our benefactor an adequate return for the mercy shown to us: a life pleasing to him
and a sober and watchful soul. This festival and celebration require no wealth,
no food, but only willingness and a clean conscience. There is nothing bodily to buy,
but everything is spiritual: listening to the words of God, a father’s prayers,
the blessings of priests, participation in God’s ineffable mysteries,
peace and unity, spiritual gifts, and gifts worthy of the beloved giver.
Let us therefore celebrate this festival on which the Lord arose. For he arose and raised the whole world with him.
He arose, breaking the bonds of death, and he raised us, loosening the fetters of our sins.
Adam sinned and died. Christ did not sin, yet died. This is new and most glorious.
The former sinned and died; the latter did not sin, yet died. For what reason, and why?
So that the one who sinned and died might, through the one who did not sin, be freed from the bonds
of death. The same thing often happens with those who owe money.
Someone owes another person money and has nothing with which to [?], and for this reason he is taken into custody.
And someone who owes nothing himself but can pay [?] gives payment and releases the debtor.
So it was with Adam and with Christ. Adam owed the debt of death
and was held captive by the devil. Christ owed no debt and was not held captive. He came and paid [?] with his death
for the captive, to release him from the bonds of death.
Have you seen the resurrection and restoration? Have you seen the Lord’s love for humanity?
Have you seen the greatness of his kindness? Let us therefore not fail to praise such a benefactor.
Nor, because the fast has passed, let us grow negligent and fail to show greater care for the soul.
Let us not allow the soul to become weaker while the flesh grows poor. Let us not care for the servant and neglect the mistress.
For tell me, what benefit is there in swelling beyond what is needed and exceeding what is enough?
This both destroys the body and betrays the soul’s nobility. Instead, let us keep to what is necessary and sufficient,
so that with both soul and body we may accomplish what is worthy, and may not lose what we have gathered through fasting—
suddenly losing it all. Am I forbidding food? I am not forbidding it, but teaching you not to exceed moderation
and to reject excessive food, lest by exceeding moderation we destroy the soul’s health.
For someone who has passed beyond the limits of necessity will no longer take pleasure in it. And this, especially,
is truly attested by those who have experienced it and have thereby acquired very many kinds of illness
and suffered much torment. But that you will obey our teaching
I do not doubt, for I know your obedience. Therefore, bringing this instruction to an end here,
to those who on this radiant night have been granted the gift of divine baptism
I wish to turn my words—to the church’s beautiful garden, its spiritual flower,
to Christ’s new soldiers. The day before yesterday the Lord was on the cross,
but now he has risen. Likewise, the day before yesterday these people were held captive under sin,
but now they have risen with Christ. He died in the body and rose in the body,
while they had been put to death by sin and have risen from sin.
Now, at this springtime, the earth brings forth roses, violets, and other flowers.
But today the waters have revealed to us a more beautiful meadow. And do not be surprised, beloved.
Though flowering meadows appeared from the waters. For in the beginning the earth did not, by its own nature, bring forth the growth of plants,
but obeyed the Master's command. And the waters, too, then brought forth moving creatures
when they heard, “Let the waters bring forth swarms of living creatures.”
And the command became reality: lifeless nature brought forth living creatures.
Likewise, now the same command has accomplished everything. Then he said, “Let the waters bring forth swarms of living creatures.”
But now it brings forth not swarming creatures but spiritual gifts. Then the waters brought forth fish without reason,
but now they have brought forth for us rational and spiritual fish, caught by the apostles.
“Come after me,” he said, “and I will make you fishers of people.”
The manner of this fishing is truly new. For fishermen always take fish out of the waters and kill them.
We put what we catch into the water, and those who are caught come to life.
There was once a pool of water among the Jews as well. But learn what it could do,
so that you may truly know the poverty of the Jews, and you will come to know our wealth.
“An angel would come down there,” it says, “and stir the water.” And whoever entered after the stirring of the water
received healing. The Master of the angels came down into the waters of the Jordan
and, having sanctified the nature of water, healed the whole world. Therefore, there,
whoever went down after the first person was no longer healed. For the gift was given to the Jews,
who were weak and crawled along the ground. But here a second person goes down after the first,
and after the second, a third and a fourth. Even if you speak of ten thousand,
even if you cast the whole world into the waters, the share will not diminish.
Have you seen the greatness of the gift? Listen, all of you enrolled in the heavenly city, Jerusalem,
today and tonight. And show care worthy of the greatness of the gifts,
so that you may also receive an abundant gift. For goodwill concerning former sins
receives a great gift from the Master. It is no longer right for you, beloved,
to live without restraint. Instead, establish a law and a rule for yourself, so that you do everything
in moderation. And show great care even in matters thought to require no restraint.
For this present life is a struggle and a battle. And those who have once entered this arena of virtue
must exercise restraint in everything. Do you not see how much effort people put into an earthly contest,
since they are wrestling with other people, and with how much self-restraint they practice bodily fasting?
So it is here as well. Since our battle is not against human beings but against spiritual forces of wickedness,
let our fasting and self-restraint also be spiritual.
For the armor with which the Master has clothed us is also spiritual.
Let the eye, then, also have discipline and moderation, so that it does not mindlessly leap at everything it sees.
And let the tongue have a wall around it, so that it does not run ahead of the mind.
For this reason the teeth and lips were made as a defense for the tongue,
so that the tongue may never simply open the doors and come out, but only when it has properly prepared itself.
Then let it come out with all grace, and let it utter such words
as will impart grace to those who hear. And let it say what benefits its hearers.
We must put away unseemly laughter [?] and have a [?] manner of walking,
and orderly clothing. And in every respect one must conduct oneself in an entirely orderly way,
as someone enrolled in the arena of virtue. For the orderly bearing of the outward parts of the body
is a kind of image of the soul’s orderly state. So if, in this manner,
we put ourselves in order from the outset as we walk along the path, we will then easily accomplish every virtue.
We will not have to undertake great toil, and we will receive much help from above. For in this way we will be able
both to sail safely across the waves of this present life and, having risen above the devil’s snares,
to obtain eternal blessings through the grace and love for humanity of our Lord Jesus Christ,
with whom glory, honor, and dominion belong to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
